segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But false prophets also arose among the people, just as there will be false teachers among you too. They will smuggle in destructive teachings, even denying the Master who bought them, and so bring swift destruction on themselves.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Many will follow them in their debauchery, and because of them the way of truth will be slandered.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In their greed they will exploit you with fabricated words. For a long time now their condemnation has not been idle, and their destruction is not asleep.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For if God did not spare angels when they sinned, but consigned them to Tartarus in chains of gloom and handed them over to be kept for judgment;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and if he did not spare the ancient world, but protected Noah, a herald of righteousness, with seven others, when he brought a flood on the world of the ungodly;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and if he condemned the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah to ruin, reducing them to ashes, and made them an example of what is coming for the ungodly;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and if he rescued righteous Lot, who was worn down by the debauched conduct of unprincipled people—

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for by what he saw and heard while living among them, that righteous man tormented his righteous soul day after day over their lawless deeds—

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: then the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trial, and how to keep the unrighteous under punishment for the day of judgment,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: especially those who go after the flesh in defiling desire and despise authority. Brazen and arrogant, they do not tremble as they slander the glorious ones,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: whereas angels, though greater in strength and power, do not bring a slanderous judgment against them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But these people, like unreasoning animals, creatures of instinct born to be caught and destroyed, slander what they do not understand, and in the destruction of those creatures they too will be destroyed,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: suffering wrong as the wages of wrongdoing. They count reveling in the daytime a pleasure. They are stains and blemishes, reveling in their deceptions as they feast with you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They have eyes full of adultery that never rest from sin; they lure unstable souls; they have hearts trained in greed. Children of a curse!

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Leaving the straight way, they have gone astray and followed the way of Balaam son of Bosor, who loved the wages of wrongdoing

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but was rebuked for his own lawbreaking: a voiceless donkey, speaking in a human voice, restrained the prophet’s madness.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: These people are waterless springs and mists driven by a storm; for them the gloom of darkness has been kept.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For, speaking swollen words of emptiness, they lure with the desires of the flesh, with debauchery, those who are barely escaping from people who live in error,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: promising them freedom while they themselves are slaves of corruption; for people are enslaved to whatever has overcome them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For if, having escaped the defilements of the world through knowledge of the Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, they are again entangled in them and overcome, their last state has become worse than their first.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For it would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness than, having known it, to turn back from the holy commandment handed on to them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What the true proverb says has happened to them:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “A dog goes back to its own vomit,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and, “A sow, once washed, goes back to wallowing in the mud.”

notes.note: The Greek word meant a chosen school of thought, a party, or its distinctive views; it was used neutrally of philosophical schools and of Jewish groups such as the Pharisees. 'Heresy' in the later sense of doctrine condemned by church authority is an anachronism here, though this verse is one of the places where the word is moving in a negative direction. Some scholars prefer 'factions' or 'sects'; most translations keep 'heresies'.

The word is the ordinary term for the owner of slaves, not the usual word for 'Lord'. The picture is of a slave purchased by a new owner and then disowning him; the 'Master' is generally taken to be Christ.

The Greek verb means to speak abusively or defame, whether the object is God, people, or things. English 'blaspheme' is now limited to speech against God, which does not fit its uses in this chapter (the way of truth, the glorious ones, things not understood). The same word-family is rendered 'slander' and 'slanderous' in verses 10–12.

The Greek is a single verb, 'to send to Tartarus', found only here in the New Testament. In Greek tradition Tartarus was the deep prison below Hades where the defeated Titans were held, and Jewish writers in Greek had adopted the name for the place where rebel angels are confined. 'Hell' blurs this with other terms; here it is a place of detention before judgment, not the final punishment. The story assumed is the Jewish tradition, built on Genesis 6:1–4, of angels who sinned before the flood.

Manuscripts are divided between two similar-looking words: 'chains' (seirais) and 'pits' (sirois). Several important early manuscripts read 'pits of gloom'; the edition translated here reads 'chains', which also matches the parallel in Jude 6. Either reading yields the same picture of imprisonment in darkness.

The Greek participle is present tense and most naturally means the unrighteous are already being punished while they are held for the day of judgment. Some scholars and translations take it with a future sense: 'to keep the unrighteous to be punished at the day of judgment'. The grammar allows either.

Literally 'glories'. Most scholars take this as a term for angelic beings, as in the parallel at Jude 8, though whether good angels or fallen ones are meant is disputed; verse 11 may suggest the latter, since even angels do not denounce 'them'. Older translations understood human or church authorities ('dignities').

Many manuscripts add 'before the Lord' after these words, and some read 'from the Lord'; others have neither phrase. The edition translated here follows the shorter text, while many translations include 'before the Lord'. 'Them' most likely refers to the glorious ones of verse 10.

notes.phrase: in the destruction of those creatures
notes.traditional: shall utterly perish in their own corruption
notes.note: The Greek says 'in their destruction they too will be destroyed', and 'their' could refer either to the animals just mentioned or to the false teachers themselves. The rendering takes it of the animals: the teachers will meet the same end as the beasts they resemble. The same Greek word is rendered 'corruption' in verse 19, where moral decay is in view; the older tradition used 'corruption' here as well.

notes.phrase: suffering wrong as the wages of wrongdoing
notes.traditional: and shall receive the reward of unrighteousness
notes.note: The reading followed here is a deliberate play on words: those who did wrong are 'wronged' in return, that is, paid back in harm. The expression is harsh, and many manuscripts have the smoother 'receiving the wages of wrongdoing'. Some interpreters take the harder reading to mean 'cheated of the wages of wrongdoing'.

Some manuscripts read 'their love feasts' (agapais) instead of 'their deceptions' (apatais), a difference of two letters in Greek. 'Love feasts' matches the parallel in Jude 12 and may have been copied from there. The mention of feasting together shows that the community's shared meals are in view in either case.

notes.traditional: Balaam the son of Bosor / Beor
notes.note: In Numbers 22–24 Balaam's father is called Beor, and a few manuscripts correct the name to that form here. 'Bosor' is the better-attested reading; why the author used it is uncertain, and one suggestion is a play on the Hebrew word for 'flesh'. Balaam was the prophet hired to curse Israel, whose donkey spoke to stop him; later Jewish tradition treated him as the type of a teacher corrupted by money.

The first saying corresponds to Proverbs 26:11, though not in the wording of the Greek Old Testament. The second is not from Scripture; similar sayings about a washed pig returning to the mud circulated in ancient wisdom literature, including versions of the story of Ahiqar. Dogs and pigs were both regarded as unclean animals.

candidates.reason: Used across the New Testament of abusive speech against God, people and things; whether to keep 'blaspheme' or use 'slander/revile' needs one rule so the English does not vary arbitrarily.
Rendered variously as 'sect', 'party', 'faction' and 'heresy' in Acts, Paul and here; 'heresy' is anachronistic, and a consistent policy by sense is needed.
Recurs in vice lists across the Gospels and letters, and translations vary between 'sensuality', 'licentiousness', 'debauchery' and 'lewdness'.
Covers physical destruction, decay and moral corruption in Paul and 2 Peter; a decision is needed on when to use 'corruption', 'decay' or 'destruction', and how to keep it distinct from ἀπώλεια.
The εὐσεβ-/ἀσεβ- family (godly/ungodly, godliness, piety, reverence) recurs in the Pastorals, Romans, Jude and 2 Peter and needs one consistent English pairing.
